\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The empirical object}
In a quadratic-sieve-type sweep one fixes $N$, sets $r=\sqrt N$, and examines
$j$ over a window of length $M$ immediately above $r$. For each $j$ the value
$v(j)=j^{2}-N$ is tested for smoothness against a factor base; a \emph{hit} is a
$j$ whose value factors as required. A heuristic model predicts the density of
hits as a function of position --- essentially a Dickman-type smoothness density
evaluated at the local value size --- and the diagnostic of interest is the
positional ratio
\[
  R(x)=\frac{T(x)}{M(x)},\qquad x\in[0,1]\ \text{the relative window position.}
\]
Across a replicated sweep of $9594$ hits over $128$ moduli, binned into $64$
equal positional bins, the measured profile is emphatically not flat.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
statistic & value\\
\midrule
$R$ at the first bin & $0.8371$\\
$R$ at the peak (bin $33$ of $64$) & $1.2227$\\
$R$ at the last bin & $0.8935$\\
pooled quadratic-fit apex (relative position) & $0.5901$\\
independent replication of the apex & $0.5896$\\
pooled fitted curvature, controls & $-0.105$ (CI straddles $0$)\\
fitted curvature, dominant band & $-0.299$\\
fitted curvatures, three descriptive sub-strata & $-0.18,\ -0.25,\ -0.44$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The excess is of order $\pm20\%$, is concave, has deficits at both edges, and
has an apex reproduced to four digits by an independent computation.

\subsection{Elimination of compositional carriers}
The natural first hypothesis is compositional: the hit population is a mixture
of sub-populations with different positional behaviour. This is excluded
arithmetically. Sorting hits by the size of the largest prime factor of $v(j)$
into the four eligible size bands, the observed masses are
\[
  [\,0,\ 0,\ 0.0007,\ 0.9993\,]\quad(\text{counts }[0,0,7,9587]),
\]
against a theoretical mixture prediction of $[\,0,0,0.0013,0.9987\,]$. A single
band carries $99.93\%$ of all hits, so there is nothing to mix, and mass
reallocation between bands (gap $6\times10^{-4}$) cannot generate a $20\%$
shaped effect. Descending inside the dominant band does not help: split
descriptively into three sub-strata, the fitted curvature is negative in all
three ($-0.18,-0.25,-0.44$). Conditioning instead on small-prime combinatorics
produces conditioned amplitudes of $\pm2\%$ against a pooled excess of $+4.8\%$.
Controls are clean throughout: hump-free synthetic data return a curvature whose
confidence interval contains zero and a peak fit of $1.005$.

What survives is the geometric channel: the hump is produced by the shape of
$j^{2}-N$ on the window, interacting with the sizes of the sieved values. This
paper is a complete analysis of what that channel can and cannot produce.

\section{The window model and the geometry of the hump}

\begin{definition}[Window coordinates]\label{def:window}
Let $N>0$, $r=\sqrt N$, and let the sieve window be $j=r+s$ with $s$ ranging
over an interval of length $M>0$. Write $x=s/M$ and
$c=r/M=\sqrt N/M\ge0$, the \emph{aspect ratio}. Then
\[
  j^{2}-N=(r+s)^{2}-r^{2}=s(s+2r)=M^{2}\,x(x+2c).
\]
We call $W_{c}(x)=x(x+2c)$ the normalised window value and
\[
  L_{c}(x)=\log x+\log(x+2c)
\]
the \emph{log-size profile}. For $c\ge0$, $x>0$ one has $W_{c}(x)>0$ and
$L_{c}(x)=\log W_{c}(x)$, the profile being the logarithm of the sieved value up
to the additive constant $2\log M$, invisible to every statistic below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Chord, chord slope, gap]
For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $a\ne b$,
\[
  \ch_{f}^{a,b}(x)=f(a)+\frac{x-a}{b-a}\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr),\qquad
  \sigma_{f}^{a,b}=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a},\qquad
  G_{f}^{a,b}(x)=f(x)-\ch_{f}^{a,b}(x).
\]
By construction $G_{f}^{a,b}(a)=G_{f}^{a,b}(b)=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Strict concavity of the log-size profile]\label{thm:concave}
For every $c\ge0$, the function $L_{c}(x)=\log x+\log(x+2c)$ is strictly concave
on $(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\log$ is strictly concave on $(0,\infty)$; $x\mapsto\log(x+2c)$ is a left
translate of $\log$ by $2c\ge0$, hence strictly concave on a set containing
$(0,\infty)$; a sum of two strictly concave functions on a convex set is
strictly concave. Equivalently $L_{c}''(x)=-x^{-2}-(x+2c)^{-2}<0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The hump exists]\label{thm:hump}
Let $f$ be strictly concave on a set $S$ and let $a,b\in S$ with $a<x<b$. Then
$G_{f}^{a,b}(x)>0$. If $f$ is merely concave then $G_{f}^{a,b}(x)\ge0$ for
$x\in[a,b]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $\theta=(b-x)/(b-a)\in(0,1)$, so $x=\theta a+(1-\theta)b$ and
$\ch_{f}^{a,b}(x)=\theta f(a)+(1-\theta)f(b)$: the chord at an interior point
\emph{is} the corresponding convex combination of endpoint values. Strict
concavity gives $f(x)>\theta f(a)+(1-\theta)f(b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Qualitative prediction of the geometric channel]
For $c\ge0$ and $0<a<x<b$ one has $G_{L_{c}}^{a,b}(x)>0$ while
$G_{L_{c}}^{a,b}(a)=G_{L_{c}}^{a,b}(b)=0$: a strictly one-signed interior excess
with exact deficits at both window edges, matching the measured pattern
$0.837$--$1.223$--$0.894$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}[Vertex]
The derivative of the log-size profile is
$L_{c}'(x)=\tfrac1x+\tfrac1{x+2c}$. A point $\xi$ is a \emph{vertex} of the hump
on $[a,b]$ if $\xi\in(a,b)$ and $L_{c}'(\xi)=\sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Existence, uniqueness and maximality of the vertex]
\label{thm:vertex}
Let $c\ge0$ and $0<a<b$. Then a vertex $\xi$ exists; it is unique; and
$G_{L_{c}}^{a,b}$ is strictly increasing on $[a,\xi]$ and strictly decreasing on
$[\xi,b]$, so $\xi$ is the unique maximiser of the gap on $[a,b]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Existence is the mean value theorem for $L_{c}$ on $[a,b]$. Uniqueness holds
because $x\mapsto x^{-1}+(x+2c)^{-1}$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$,
hence injective. The gap has derivative $L_{c}'(x)-\sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}$, which
is positive for $x<\xi$ and negative for $x>\xi$ by the same strict
antitonicity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Degenerate aspect ratio]\label{thm:c0}
For $c=0$ and $0<a<b$ the unique vertex is the logarithmic mean
\[
  \xi=\LM(a,b):=\frac{b-a}{\log b-\log a}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
At $c=0$, $L_{0}=2\log$, so $L_{0}'(\xi)=2/\xi$ and
$\sigma_{L_{0}}^{a,b}=2(\log b-\log a)/(b-a)$; equate and solve. As a
by-product $a<\LM(a,b)<b$.
\end{proof}

\section{The fitted curvature is a certificate of concavity}

\begin{definition}[Fitted curvature]
Given sample points $t_{0},\dots,t_{n-1}$, a quadratic $q$ and a profile $g$,
\[
  \widehat c(g)=\frac{\sum_{i<n}g(t_{i})q(t_{i})}{\sum_{i<n}q(t_{i})^{2}},
\]
where $q$ is \emph{grid-orthogonal}: $\sum_{i<n}q(t_{i})=0$ and
$\sum_{i<n}t_{i}q(t_{i})=0$. These are precisely the normal equations making
$\widehat c$ the least-squares quadratic coefficient of $g$ on the grid.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Chord bridge]\label{lem:bridge}
For any $g$ and $r_{1}<r_{2}<y$,
\[
  \ch_{g}^{r_{1},r_{2}}(y)-g(y)=\frac{y-r_{1}}{r_{2}-r_{1}}\,G_{g}^{r_{1},y}(r_{2}),
\]
and symmetrically, for $y<r_{1}<r_{2}$,
$\ch_{g}^{r_{1},r_{2}}(y)-g(y)=\frac{r_{2}-y}{r_{2}-r_{1}}G_{g}^{y,r_{2}}(r_{1})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Pure algebra: both sides measure the same triangle. Clearing denominators
reduces the claim to a polynomial identity in
$g(r_{1}),g(r_{2}),g(y),r_{1},r_{2},y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sign pattern of the chord residual]\label{thm:signptwise}
Let $g$ be concave on $S$, $r_{1}<r_{2}$ in $S$, $y\in S$. Then
\[
  \bigl(g(y)-\ch_{g}^{r_{1},r_{2}}(y)\bigr)\cdot\bigl((y-r_{1})(y-r_{2})\bigr)\le0,
\]
strictly if $g$ is strictly concave and $y\notin\{r_{1},r_{2}\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Three cases. For $r_{1}\le y\le r_{2}$ the residual is $\ge0$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:hump} and $(y-r_{1})(y-r_{2})\le0$. For $y>r_{2}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:bridge} (right form) with non-negativity of
$G_{g}^{r_{1},y}(r_{2})$ makes the residual $\le0$ while the quadratic is $>0$.
The case $y<r_{1}$ is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Affine profiles score zero]\label{lem:affzero}
If $q(y)=(y-r_{1})(y-r_{2})$ is grid-orthogonal then
$\sum_{i<n}(u+vt_{i})q(t_{i})=0$ for all $u,v$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Sign theorem]\label{thm:sign}
Let $g$ be concave on $S$, $r_{1}<r_{2}$ in $S$, and $t_{0},\dots,t_{n-1}\in S$
with $q(y)=(y-r_{1})(y-r_{2})$ grid-orthogonal. Then
$\sum_{i<n}g(t_{i})q(t_{i})\le0$, strictly if $g$ is strictly concave and some
$t_{i}\notin\{r_{1},r_{2}\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Split $g=(g-\ch_{g}^{r_{1},r_{2}})+\ch_{g}^{r_{1},r_{2}}$. The chord is affine
and contributes $0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:affzero}; each remaining term is $\le0$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:signptwise}.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The pipeline grid.}
For $n$ bins of width $h>0$ centred at $m$ set
\[
  o_{i}=i-\frac{n-1}{2},\qquad t_{i}=m+h\,o_{i},\qquad
  V(n)=\frac1n\sum_{i<n}o_{i}^{2},\qquad \rho=h\sqrt{V(n)},
\]
and $r_{1,2}=m\mp\rho$, so that $q(y)=(y-m)^{2}-h^{2}V(n)$.

\begin{theorem}[The bin grid is orthogonal, at every width and centre]
\label{thm:orth}
For $n\ge2$, every $h$ and every $m$,
$\sum_{i<n}q(t_{i})=0$ and $\sum_{i<n}t_{i}q(t_{i})=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$q(t_{i})=h^{2}(o_{i}^{2}-V(n))$, so the first sum vanishes by definition of
$V$. For the second, $t_{i}q(t_{i})=m h^{2}(o_{i}^{2}-V(n))+h^{3}(o_{i}^{3}-V(n)o_{i})$;
the first bracket sums to $0$ as before, and $\sum o_{i}^{3}=\sum o_{i}=0$ since
the reflection $i\mapsto n-1-i$ sends $o_{i}\mapsto-o_{i}$ and both $y$ and
$y^{3}$ are odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A witness bin]\label{lem:witness}
For $n\ge3$ and $h>0$ at least one of $t_{0},t_{1}$ avoids both roots, because
$o_{0}^{2}\ne o_{1}^{2}$ and $q(t_{i})=h^{2}(o_{i}^{2}-V(n))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Bin-width and grid-shift invariance of the measured sign]
\label{thm:fitneg}
Let $g$ be strictly concave on $S$, $n\ge3$, $h>0$, $m$ arbitrary, with
$r_{1},r_{2}$ and all $t_{i}$ in $S$. Then $\sum_{i<n}g(t_{i})q(t_{i})<0$ and
hence $\widehat c(g)<0$. In particular, for the log-size profile $L_{c}$ of
$j^{2}-N$ and any equal-width bin grid inside the window, $\widehat c(L_{c})<0$
for every bin count $n\ge3$, every bin width $h>0$ and every grid centre $m$;
whereas an affine profile yields $\widehat c=0$ exactly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:concave}, \ref{thm:sign}, \ref{thm:orth} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:witness}; the denominator is positive since $q(t_{i})\ne0$ for
some $i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This discharges the pre-registered ``bin-width permutation / grid shift'' probe
as a theorem rather than a simulation: a measured $\widehat c<0$ cannot be a
grid accident, and a measured $\widehat c=0$ on controls is exactly what an
affine profile must produce. The observed values
$-0.105,-0.18,-0.25,-0.299,-0.44$ are genuine certificates of concavity of
$\log(j^{2}-N)$.
\end{remark}

\section{Binning cannot create, destroy, or split the hump}

\begin{definition}[Sample grid and bin averages]
For offset $a$, spacing $\delta$ and bin width $w\ge1$ the samples are
$s_{i}=a+\delta i$ and the binned profile is
$b_{k}=\frac1w\sum_{i<w}g(s_{kw+i})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Midpoint alignment]\label{lem:mid}
For all $k,i,w$: $s_{kw+i}+s_{(k+2)w+i}=2s_{(k+1)w+i}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Binning preserves concavity]\label{thm:binconc}
Let $g$ be concave on $S$ with all samples in $S$. Then for every offset $a$,
every spacing $\delta$, every bin width $w$ and every $k$,
\[
  b_{k}+b_{k+2}\le 2b_{k+1},
\]
strictly if $g$ is strictly concave, $w\ge1$ and $\delta\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Midpoint concavity gives $g(u)+g(v)\le2g\bigl(\tfrac{u+v}{2}\bigr)$; apply with
$u=s_{kw+i}$, $v=s_{(k+2)w+i}$, whose midpoint is $s_{(k+1)w+i}$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:mid}. Sum over $i<w$ and divide by $w>0$. Strictness needs
$u\ne v$, which holds as $\delta\ne0$ and the indices differ by $2w\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Control: binning an affine profile]\label{thm:binaff}
For $g(y)=u+vy$ one has $b_{k}+b_{k+2}-2b_{k+1}=0$ identically, for every
$a,\delta,w,k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Discrete concavity forces unimodality]\label{thm:unimodal}
Let $(b_{k})$ satisfy $b_{k}+b_{k+2}\le2b_{k+1}$ for all $k$ and suppose
$b_{k+1}\le b_{k}$ for some $k$. Then $b_{k+j+1}\le b_{k+j}$ for all $j\ge0$:
once the sequence descends it never ascends again.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $j$: discrete concavity at index $k+j$ gives
$b_{k+j+2}\le2b_{k+j+1}-b_{k+j}\le b_{k+j+1}$ using the inductive hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The sieve instance]
For $c\ge0$, any offset $a$ and spacing $\delta\ne0$ with all samples positive,
and any bin width $w\ge1$, the binned log-size profile of $j^{2}-N$ satisfies
$b_{k}+b_{k+2}<2b_{k+1}$ for all $k$ and is unimodal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
No bin-width permutation and no grid shift can split the measured peak into two,
nor manufacture a peak where the underlying profile is affine. Concavity and
single-peakedness of $R$ are grid invariants of any concave underlying profile.
\end{remark}

\section{The obstruction: geometry puts the vertex left of centre}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp log inequality]\label{thm:logineq}
For $t>1$, $\displaystyle \frac{2(t-1)}{t+1}<\log t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Set $f(t)=\log t-2(t-1)/(t+1)$; then $f(1)=0$ and
$f'(t)=\tfrac1t-\tfrac4{(t+1)^{2}}=\tfrac{(t-1)^{2}}{t(t+1)^{2}}>0$ for $t>1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$\LM<\mathrm{AM}$]\label{cor:lmam}
For $0<p<q$,
$\displaystyle \frac{2}{p+q}<\frac{\log q-\log p}{q-p}$, i.e.
$\LM(p,q)<\frac{p+q}{2}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Main obstruction]\label{thm:obstruction}
For every $c\ge0$ and every window $0<a<b$ the unique vertex satisfies
\[
  \xi<\frac{a+b}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $m=(a+b)/2$. The chord slope splits into the two factor slopes,
\[
  \sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}
  =\frac{\log b-\log a}{b-a}
  +\frac{\log(b+2c)-\log(a+2c)}{(b+2c)-(a+2c)} .
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:lmam} applied to $(a,b)$ and to $(a+2c,b+2c)$ bounds the two
summands below by $1/m$ and $1/(m+2c)$ respectively. Hence
$L_{c}'(m)<\sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}=L_{c}'(\xi)$, and since $L_{c}'$ is strictly
decreasing, $\xi<m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Normalised form]
$(\xi-a)/(b-a)<1/2$; consequently the geometric vertex can never equal the
measured relative apex $0.5901$ (replicated at $0.5896$), for any $N$, any
window and any aspect ratio.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative collapse to the left edge]\label{thm:collapse}
For $0<a<b$,
\[
  \frac{\LM(a,b)-a}{b-a}=\frac{1}{\log b-\log a}-\frac{a}{b-a}
  \le\frac{1}{\log(b/a)} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
In the sieve regime $a=1/M$, $b=1$ this reads $\le 1/\log M$: as the window
lengthens the geometric vertex is pushed \emph{toward the left edge}, not toward
$0.59$. The measured value is not a near miss; the discrepancy grows with
problem size.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Control: a purely quadratic profile peaks at the centre]
For $f(y)=-y^{2}$ and $a<b$, $G_{f}^{a,b}(x)=-(x-a)(x-b)$, whose maximum over
$[a,b]$ is attained exactly at $x=(a+b)/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Direct computation of the chord; the resulting inequality is equivalent to
$\bigl(x-\tfrac{a+b}{2}\bigr)^{2}\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\section{Rigidity of the vertex: a two-sided logarithmic-mean pin}

\begin{theorem}[Elementary inequality]\label{thm:elem}
For $s>1$, $\ \log s<\tfrac12\bigl(s-1/s\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$G(s)=\tfrac12(s-1/s)-\log s$ satisfies $G(1)=0$ and
$G'(s)=\tfrac{1+s^{-2}}{2}-\tfrac1s=\tfrac{(s-1)^{2}}{2s^{2}}>0$ for $s>1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Geometric mean below logarithmic mean]\label{thm:gmlm}
For $0<p<q$, $\ \sqrt{pq}\,(\log q-\log p)<q-p$, i.e. $\sqrt{pq}<\LM(p,q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute $s=\sqrt{q/p}>1$, so $q=ps^{2}$, $\sqrt{pq}=ps$ and
$\log q-\log p=2\log s$; the claim becomes $2s\log s<s^{2}-1$, which is
Theorem~\ref{thm:elem} multiplied by $2s>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shift rigidity of the logarithmic mean]\label{thm:shift}
For $0<a<b$ and $t\ge0$,
\[
  \LM(a,b)+t\le\LM(a+t,\,b+t).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix $d=b-a$, set $D(u)=\log(b+u)-\log(a+u)$ and $F(u)=d/D(u)-u$ for $u\ge0$;
then $F(0)=\LM(a,b)$ and $F(t)=\LM(a+t,b+t)-t$. Differentiating,
\[
  F'(u)=\frac{-d\bigl((b+u)^{-1}-(a+u)^{-1}\bigr)}{D(u)^{2}}-1
       =\frac{d^{2}-(a+u)(b+u)D(u)^{2}}{(a+u)(b+u)D(u)^{2}},
\]
whose numerator is positive exactly because
$\sqrt{(a+u)(b+u)}\,D(u)<d$, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:gmlm} for the shifted
pair. Hence $F$ is strictly increasing and $F(0)\le F(t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Chord slope in terms of logarithmic means]\label{lem:slopesplit}
For $0<a<b$ and $c\ge0$,
\[
  \sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}=\frac1{\LM(a,b)}+\frac1{\LM(a+2c,\,b+2c)} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided pin]\label{thm:pin}
For $c\ge0$ and $0<a<b$,
\[
  \LM(a,b)\;\le\;\xi\;\le\;\LM(a+2c,\,b+2c)-2c\;<\;\frac{a+b}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $L=\LM(a,b)$, $L_{2}=\LM(a+2c,b+2c)$; Theorem~\ref{thm:shift} with $t=2c$
gives $L+2c\le L_{2}$. Lower pin: by Lemma~\ref{lem:slopesplit} and
$1/L_{2}\le1/(L+2c)$,
$\sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}\le\tfrac1L+\tfrac1{L+2c}=L_{c}'(L)$, so
$L_{c}'(\xi)\le L_{c}'(L)$ and hence $\xi\ge L$ by strict antitonicity. Upper
pin: $L_{c}'(L_{2}-2c)=\tfrac1{L_{2}-2c}+\tfrac1{L_{2}}\le\tfrac1L+\tfrac1{L_{2}}
=L_{c}'(\xi)$, so $\xi\le L_{2}-2c$. The last inequality is
Theorem~\ref{thm:obstruction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Aspect-ratio insensitivity]\label{thm:insens}
For any two aspect ratios $c_{1},c_{2}\ge0$ on the same window,
\[
  |\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}|<\frac{a+b}{2}-\LM(a,b),
\]
an interval independent of the aspect ratio.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
The lower pin is aspect-ratio free; this is the theorem behind the numerically
observed near-constancy of the vertex under variation of $c$. For the window
$[0.01,1]$ the vertex stays within $3\times10^{-2}$ of
$\LM(0.01,1)=0.214976$ as $c$ ranges over $[10^{-3},10^{9}]$.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Vertex location by monotone bisection.}
Since $L_{c}'$ is strictly decreasing, the residual
$L_{c}'(x)-\sigma_{L_{c}}^{a,b}$ changes sign exactly once on $(a,b)$;
bisection converges unconditionally, the bracket having width $(b-a)2^{-k}$
after $k$ steps. Cost $O(k)$ evaluations of $O(1)$ each.

\paragraph{Fitted curvature on an arbitrary bin grid.}
Given $n,h,m$, compute the centred offsets $o_{i}$, the grid variance $V(n)$ and
$q(y)=(y-m)^{2}-h^{2}V(n)$; then
$\widehat c=\sum g(t_{i})q(t_{i})/\sum q(t_{i})^{2}$. Cost $O(n)$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:orth} makes explicit orthogonalisation unnecessary;
Theorem~\ref{thm:fitneg} fixes the sign of the output for concave inputs, so the
routine doubles as a numerical falsification test.

\paragraph{Bin-average second differences.}
Given $a,\delta,w$, form $b_{k}$ and $b_{k}+b_{k+2}-2b_{k+1}$. Cost $O(w)$ per
bin. Theorems~\ref{thm:binconc}--\ref{thm:binaff} predict strictly negative
output on the log-size profile and machine-zero output on affine controls at
every $(a,\delta,w)$: a direct implementation of the bin-width permutation and
grid-shift probe.

\paragraph{A numerical caveat.}
The upper pin $\LM(a+2c,b+2c)-2c$ suffers catastrophic cancellation for large
$c$. With $p=a+2c$, $d=b-a$, $u=d/p$ the stable form is
\[
  \LM(p,p+d)-2c=a+d\left(\frac1{\log(1+u)}-\frac1u\right),\qquad
  \frac1{\log(1+u)}-\frac1u=\frac12-\frac{u}{12}+\frac{u^{2}}{24}-\cdots,
\]
the series being used for small $u$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What has been settled}
The mid-window excess in the yield ratio is shaped by the polynomial. The strict
concavity of $\log(j^{2}-N)$ forces, against an affine reference, a strictly
positive interior deviation vanishing at both edges with exactly one interior
peak. Every measured feature of the arch other than its apex position follows:
the sign of the excess, the deficits at both edges, the single peak, the
negative fitted curvature in every stratum, the exact-zero curvature on affine
controls and the invariance of all of this to the binning. Robustness probes of
this kind are usually run empirically; here the probe is discharged as a theorem
valid at every bin count, bin width and grid offset simultaneously, so no
untried grid could have dissolved the arch.

\subsection{What has been refuted}
The same geometry cannot place the apex. Theorem~\ref{thm:obstruction} is
universal in the two free parameters of the model and one-sided; the
quantitative refinement (Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}) shows the failure is not
marginal, the normalised apex being at most $1/\log M$ in the sieve regime while
the measurement returns $0.5901$ twice independently. Two escapes are also
closed: a pure quadratic profile peaks exactly at the midpoint, and the rigidity
result shows there is no exotic aspect ratio pushing the vertex right, the lower
pin not involving $c$ at all. The elimination is structural, not power-limited:
it does not say the data are too noisy to decide, it says no parameter setting of
this mechanism produces the measured value.

\subsection{Relation to the pre-registered analysis}
The reported statistical verdict of the underlying experiment was, by the letter
of its own pre-registration, inconclusive: no decomposition family cleared the
bar requiring a fitted-peak bootstrap lower confidence bound above $1.05$
(achieved bounds $1.0094$--$1.0275$, despite a raw maximum of $1.2227$ at bin
$33$), and the bars were kept verbatim. The present analysis does not alter that
verdict; it operates on a different axis. It establishes that the
\emph{structure} of the effect --- one-signedness, edge deficits, unimodality,
negative curvature, grid invariance --- is a theorem about $\log(j^{2}-N)$, and
that the \emph{location} of the apex is not.

\subsection{Scope and caveats}
Three limitations should be recorded. First, the reference profile is taken to
be affine on the window; a reference with curvature of its own would shift the
analysis, and the theorems then apply to the difference of curvatures. Second,
the value-size dependence of the smoothness model enters only through
$\log(j^{2}-N)$; a strongly non-logarithmic dependence is outside the scope of
Definition~\ref{def:window}. Third, sub-stratification of the dominant band is
descriptive only and licenses no threshold decision. None of these touches the
obstruction, which is a statement about $x\mapsto\log x+\log(x+2c)$ and nothing
else.

\section{Future work}

The natural next question is sharpness. Numerically the vertex hugs the lower
pin $\LM(a,b)$ to four digits for every aspect ratio, so all the slack in
Theorem~\ref{thm:pin} lives in the upper pin. A sharp upper bound
$\xi\le\LM(a,b)+\varepsilon(a,b,c)$ with explicit small $\varepsilon$ would turn
the two-sided pin into an asymptotic identity and make the aspect-ratio
insensitivity quantitative.

Beyond that the open problem is now precisely posed: some mechanism moves an
apex that all available window geometry pins to the left edge over to relative
position $0.59$. Candidates worth formalising include curvature in the reference
model itself, arising from the value-size dependence of the smoothness density
rather than from the polynomial; boundary effects of the factor base, which act
asymmetrically across the window because the small-prime root pattern of
$j^{2}\equiv N$ is not translation invariant; and genuinely arithmetic
non-uniformity in the distribution of smooth values, invisible to size-based
models. Any candidate must reproduce four things at once --- concave sign, two
edge deficits, single peak, apex right of centre --- and by the results above
the first three come free from concavity, so a candidate mechanism only has to
explain the fourth without destroying the first three.

\appendix

"""
Numerical demonstration of the window-geometry theory of the sieve hump.

Everything below is self-contained (standard library only) and illustrates,
with explicit numbers, the four theoretical pillars:

  1. LOG-SIZE CONCAVITY.  On a sieve window j = r + s with r = sqrt(N), the
     normalised value of the sieve polynomial is

         (j^2 - N) / M^2 = x (x + 2c),      x = s/M,   c = r/M,

     so the log-size profile is  L_c(x) = log x + log(x + 2c),  which is
     strictly concave.  Measured against the chord through the two window
     endpoints it produces a strictly positive interior "hump" vanishing at
     both edges, with a unique interior vertex.

  2. CURVATURE INVARIANCE.  The least-squares quadratic coefficient of a
     concave profile, taken against the grid-orthogonal quadratic
     q(y) = (y-m)^2 - h^2 V(n), is strictly negative for EVERY bin count,
     EVERY bin width h and EVERY grid centre m; for an affine profile it is
     exactly zero.

  3. BINNING INVARIANCE.  Averaging a concave profile into equal-width bins
     yields a discretely concave sequence (second differences < 0) at every
     bin width and grid offset, hence a unimodal binned profile with a single
     peak.  An affine profile bins to second difference exactly 0.

  4. THE VERTEX OBSTRUCTION AND ITS RIGIDITY.  The vertex always satisfies

         LM(a,b)  <=  xi  <=  LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c  <  (a+b)/2,
         LM(p,q) = (q-p)/(log q - log p),

     so its normalised position is always strictly below 1/2, and in the sieve
     regime a = 1/M, b = 1 it is at most 1/log M -- it collapses onto the LEFT
     edge.  The measured pooled vertex 0.5901 lies to the RIGHT of centre and
     is therefore not producible by window geometry.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The window profile
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def window_value(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Normalised sieve value (j^2 - N)/M^2 at relative window position x."""
    return x * (x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Log-size profile log x + log(x + 2c) = log((j^2 - N)/M^2)."""
    return math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size_deriv(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Derivative 1/x + 1/(x + 2c) of the log-size profile."""
    return 1.0 / x + 1.0 / (x + 2.0 * c)


def chord(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Affine reference through the two window endpoints."""
    return f(a) + (x - a) / (b - a) * (f(b) - f(a))


def chord_slope(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float) -> float:
    return (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a)


def gap(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Chord-referenced deviation: the hump."""
    return f(x) - chord(f, a, b, x)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Means and the vertex
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def log_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    """Logarithmic mean LM(p,q) = (q-p)/(log q - log p)."""
    if abs(q - p) < 1e-15:
        return p
    return (q - p) / (math.log(q) - math.log(p))


def geometric_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(p * q)


def vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float, iters: int = 200) -> float:
    """Unique xi in (a,b) with 1/xi + 1/(xi+2c) = chord slope, by bisection.

    The map x -> 1/x + 1/(x+2c) is strictly decreasing, so bisection on the
    monotone residual converges to the unique root.
    """
    s = chord_slope(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b)
    lo, hi = a, b
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if log_size_deriv(c, mid) > s:
            lo = mid           # derivative too large => move right
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def normalised_vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    return (vertex(c, a, b) - a) / (b - a)


def shifted_log_mean_upper_pin(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c, evaluated stably for very large c.

    Writing p = a + 2c, d = b - a, u = d/p, one has
        LM(p, p+d) - 2c = a + d * (1/log(1+u) - 1/u),
    and for small u the bracket is 1/2 - u/12 + u^2/24 - ..., which avoids the
    catastrophic cancellation of the naive formula.
    """
    p = a + 2.0 * c
    d = b - a
    u = d / p
    if u < 1e-4:
        bracket = 0.5 - u / 12.0 + u * u / 24.0
    else:
        bracket = 1.0 / math.log1p(u) - 1.0 / u
    return a + d * bracket


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Binning and the fitted curvature statistic
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def offsets(n: int) -> List[float]:
    """Centred index offsets i - (n-1)/2 of an n-bin grid."""
    return [i - (n - 1) / 2.0 for i in range(n)]


def grid_var(n: int) -> float:
    """Mean square centred offset of the n-bin grid."""
    off = offsets(n)
    return sum(o * o for o in off) / n


def bin_grid(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> List[float]:
    """Bin centres: n bins of width h about the grid centre m."""
    return [m + h * o for o in offsets(n)]


def orthogonal_quadratic(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """q(y) = (y-m)^2 - h^2 V(n): orthogonal to constants and to y on the grid."""
    v = grid_var(n)

    def q(y: float) -> float:
        return (y - m) ** 2 - h * h * v

    return q


def fit_curvature(
    grid: Sequence[float], q: Callable[[float], float], g: Callable[[float], float]
) -> float:
    """Least-squares quadratic coefficient of g against the orthogonal q."""
    num = sum(g(t) * q(t) for t in grid)
    den = sum(q(t) ** 2 for t in grid)
    return num / den


def bin_average(
    a: float, delta: float, w: int, g: Callable[[float], float], k: int
) -> float:
    """Average of g over the w samples a + delta*(k*w + i), i < w."""
    return sum(g(a + delta * (k * w + i)) for i in range(w)) / w


def second_difference(b: Callable[[int], float], k: int) -> float:
    """b(k) + b(k+2) - 2 b(k+1); negative means discretely concave."""
    return b(k) + b(k + 2) - 2.0 * b(k + 1)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_hump_shape(c: float = 1.0, a: float = 0.02, b: float = 1.0) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE HUMP: chord-referenced deviation of the log-size profile")
    print(f"   aspect ratio c = {c},  window [a,b] = [{a}, {b}]")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'x':>10}{'log-size':>14}{'chord':>14}{'gap':>14}")
    for i in range(11):
        x = a + (b - a) * i / 10.0
        print(
            f"{x:10.4f}{log_size(c, x):14.6f}"
            f"{chord(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, x):14.6f}"
            f"{gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, x):14.6f}"
        )
    xi = vertex(c, a, b)
    print(f"\n   edge gaps: gap(a) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, a):.3e}, "
          f"gap(b) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, b):.3e}   (both zero)")
    print(f"   vertex xi = {xi:.6f},  normalised (xi-a)/(b-a) = "
          f"{(xi - a) / (b - a):.6f}   (< 0.5)")
    print(f"   peak height gap(xi) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, xi):.6f}")


def demo_curvature_invariance(c: float = 1.0) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. FITTED CURVATURE IS NEGATIVE AT EVERY BIN WIDTH AND OFFSET")
    print("   (affine control fits to exactly zero)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'n bins':>8}{'width h':>12}{'centre m':>12}"
          f"{'c_fit(log-size)':>20}{'c_fit(affine)':>18}")
    for n, h, m in [
        (8, 0.05, 0.50),
        (16, 0.05, 0.50),
        (32, 0.02, 0.40),
        (64, 0.01, 0.35),
        (64, 0.012, 0.60),
        (17, 0.03, 0.55),
    ]:
        grid = bin_grid(n, m, h)
        if min(grid) <= 0 or m - h * math.sqrt(grid_var(n)) <= 0:
            continue
        q = orthogonal_quadratic(n, m, h)
        c_log = fit_curvature(grid, q, lambda y: log_size(c, y))
        c_aff = fit_curvature(grid, q, lambda y: 3.0 + 1.7 * y)
        print(f"{n:8d}{h:12.4f}{m:12.4f}{c_log:20.8f}{c_aff:18.2e}")


def demo_bin_invariance(c: float = 1.0) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. BINNING PRESERVES CONCAVITY (and kills nothing, creates nothing)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'offset a':>10}{'spacing d':>12}{'bin width w':>13}"
          f"{'max 2nd diff (log-size)':>26}{'affine':>12}")
    for a0, delta, w in [
        (0.01, 0.002, 1),
        (0.01, 0.002, 3),
        (0.01, 0.002, 8),
        (0.05, 0.001, 5),
        (0.13, 0.0007, 11),
    ]:
        g = lambda y: log_size(c, y)                      # noqa: E731
        aff = lambda y: -2.0 + 0.9 * y                    # noqa: E731
        b_log = lambda k: bin_average(a0, delta, w, g, k)  # noqa: E731
        b_aff = lambda k: bin_average(a0, delta, w, aff, k)  # noqa: E731
        worst = max(second_difference(b_log, k) for k in range(0, 20))
        worst_aff = max(abs(second_difference(b_aff, k)) for k in range(0, 20))
        print(f"{a0:10.3f}{delta:12.4f}{w:13d}{worst:26.3e}{worst_aff:12.1e}")
    print("   (log-size column strictly negative everywhere; affine column ~0)")

    # unimodality: once the binned profile descends it never rises again.
    # The chord-referenced deviation is concave (concave minus affine), and it
    # is the object that actually humps.
    a0, b0 = 0.01, 1.0
    g = lambda y: gap(lambda z: log_size(c, z), a0, b0, y)  # noqa: E731
    seq = [bin_average(a0, 0.004, 4, g, k) for k in range(60)]
    peak = max(range(len(seq)), key=lambda k: seq[k])
    rises_after_peak = sum(
        1 for k in range(peak, len(seq) - 1) if seq[k + 1] > seq[k]
    )

"""
Numerical demonstration of the window-geometry theory of the sieve hump.

Everything below is self-contained (standard library only) and illustrates,
with explicit numbers, the four theoretical pillars:

  1. LOG-SIZE CONCAVITY.  On a sieve window j = r + s with r = sqrt(N), the
     normalised value of the sieve polynomial is

         (j^2 - N) / M^2 = x (x + 2c),      x = s/M,   c = r/M,

     so the log-size profile is  L_c(x) = log x + log(x + 2c),  which is
     strictly concave.  Measured against the chord through the two window
     endpoints it produces a strictly positive interior "hump" vanishing at
     both edges, with a unique interior vertex.

  2. CURVATURE INVARIANCE.  The least-squares quadratic coefficient of a
     concave profile, taken against the grid-orthogonal quadratic
     q(y) = (y-m)^2 - h^2 V(n), is strictly negative for EVERY bin count,
     EVERY bin width h and EVERY grid centre m; for an affine profile it is
     exactly zero.

  3. BINNING INVARIANCE.  Averaging a concave profile into equal-width bins
     yields a discretely concave sequence (second differences < 0) at every
     bin width and grid offset, hence a unimodal binned profile with a single
     peak.  An affine profile bins to second difference exactly 0.

  4. THE VERTEX OBSTRUCTION AND ITS RIGIDITY.  The vertex always satisfies

         LM(a,b)  <=  xi  <=  LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c  <  (a+b)/2,
         LM(p,q) = (q-p)/(log q - log p),

     so its normalised position is always strictly below 1/2, and in the sieve
     regime a = 1/M, b = 1 it is at most 1/log M -- it collapses onto the LEFT
     edge.  The measured pooled vertex 0.5901 lies to the RIGHT of centre and
     is therefore not producible by window geometry.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The window profile
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def window_value(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Normalised sieve value (j^2 - N)/M^2 at relative window position x."""
    return x * (x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Log-size profile log x + log(x + 2c) = log((j^2 - N)/M^2)."""
    return math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size_deriv(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Derivative 1/x + 1/(x + 2c) of the log-size profile."""
    return 1.0 / x + 1.0 / (x + 2.0 * c)


def chord(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Affine reference through the two window endpoints."""
    return f(a) + (x - a) / (b - a) * (f(b) - f(a))


def chord_slope(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float) -> float:
    return (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a)


def gap(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Chord-referenced deviation: the hump."""
    return f(x) - chord(f, a, b, x)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Means and the vertex
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def log_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    """Logarithmic mean LM(p,q) = (q-p)/(log q - log p)."""
    if abs(q - p) < 1e-15:
        return p
    return (q - p) / (math.log(q) - math.log(p))


def geometric_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(p * q)


def vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float, iters: int = 200) -> float:
    """Unique xi in (a,b) with 1/xi + 1/(xi+2c) = chord slope, by bisection.

    The map x -> 1/x + 1/(x+2c) is strictly decreasing, so bisection on the
    monotone residual converges to the unique root.
    """
    s = chord_slope(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b)
    lo, hi = a, b
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if log_size_deriv(c, mid) > s:
            lo = mid           # derivative too large => move right
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def normalised_vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    return (vertex(c, a, b) - a) / (b - a)


def shifted_log_mean_upper_pin(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c, evaluated stably for very large c.

    Writing p = a + 2c, d = b - a, u = d/p, one has
        LM(p, p+d) - 2c = a + d * (1/log(1+u) - 1/u),
    and for small u the bracket is 1/2 - u/12 + u^2/24 - ..., which avoids the
    catastrophic cancellation of the naive formula.
    """
    p = a + 2.0 * c
    d = b - a
    u = d / p
    if u < 1e-4:
        bracket = 0.5 - u / 12.0 + u * u / 24.0
    else:
        bracket = 1.0 / math.log1p(u) - 1.0 / u
    return a + d * bracket


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Binning and the fitted curvature statistic
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def offsets(n: int) -> List[float]:
    """Centred index offsets i - (n-1)/2 of an n-bin grid."""
    return [i - (n - 1) / 2.0 for i in range(n)]


def grid_var(n: int) -> float:
    """Mean square centred offset of the n-bin grid."""
    off = offsets(n)
    return sum(o * o for o in off) / n


def bin_grid(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> List[float]:
    """Bin centres: n bins of width h about the grid centre m."""
    return [m + h * o for o in offsets(n)]


def orthogonal_quadratic(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """q(y) = (y-m)^2 - h^2 V(n): orthogonal to constants and to y on the grid."""
    v = grid_var(n)

    def q(y: float) -> float:
        return (y - m) ** 2 - h * h * v

    return q


def fit_curvature(
    grid: Sequence[float], q: Callable[[float], float], g: Callable[[float], float]
) -> float:
    """Least-squares quadratic coefficient of g against the orthogonal q."""
    num = sum(g(t) * q(t) for t in grid)
    den = sum(q(t) ** 2 for t in grid)
    return num / den


def bin_average(
    a: float, delta: float, w: int, g: Callable[[float], float], k: int
) -> float:
    """Average of g over the w samples a + delta*(k*w + i), i < w."""
    return sum(g(a + delta * (k * w + i)) for i in range(w)) / w


def second_difference(b: Callable[[int], float], k: int) -> float:
    """b(k) + b(k+2) - 2 b(k+1); negative means discretely concave."""
    return b(k) + b(k + 2) - 2.0 * b(k + 1)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_hump_shape(c: float = 1.0, a: float = 0.02, b: float = 1.0) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE HUMP: chord-referenced deviation of the log-size profile")
    print(f"   aspect ratio c = {c},  window [a,b] = [{a}, {b}]")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'x':>10}{'log-size':>14}{'chord':>14}{'gap':>14}")
    for i in range(11):
        x = a + (b - a) * i / 10.0
        print(
            f"{x:10.4f}{log_size(c, x):14.6f}"
            f"{chord(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, x):14.6f}"
            f"{gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, x):14.6f}"
        )
    xi = vertex(c, a, b)
    print(f"\n   edge gaps: gap(a) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, a):.3e}, "
          f"gap(b) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, b):.3e}   (both zero)")
    print(f"   vertex xi = {xi:.6f},  normalised (xi-a)/(b-a) = "
          f"{(xi - a) / (b - a):.6f}   (< 0.5)")
    print(f"   peak height gap(xi) = {gap(lambda y: log_size(c, y), a, b, xi):.6f}")


def demo_curvature_invariance(c: float = 1.0) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. FITTED CURVATURE IS NEGATIVE AT EVERY BIN WIDTH AND OFFSET")
    print("   (affine control fits to exactly zero)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'n bins':>8}{'width h':>12}{'centre m':>12}"
          f"{'c_fit(log-size)':>20}{'c_fit(affine)':>18}")
    for n, h, m in [
        (8, 0.05, 0.50),
        (16, 0.05, 0.50),
        (32, 0.02, 0.40),
        (64, 0.01, 0.35),
        (64, 0.012, 0.60),
        (17, 0.03, 0.55),
    ]:
        grid = bin_grid(n, m, h)
        if min(grid) <= 0 or m - h * math.sqrt(grid_var(n)) <= 0:
            continue
        q = orthogonal_quadratic(n, m, h)
        c_log = fit_curvature(grid, q, lambda y: log_size(c, y))
        c_aff = fit_curvature(grid, q, lambda y: 3.0 + 1.7 * y)
        print(f"{n:8d}{h:12.4f}{m:12.4f}{c_log:20.8f}{c_aff:18.2e}")

    print()

    print("3. BINNING PRESERVES CONCAVITY (and kills nothing, creates nothing)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'offset a':>10}{'spacing d':>12}{'bin width w':>13}"
          f"{'max 2nd diff (log-size)':>26}{'affine':>12}")
    for a0, delta, w in [
        (0.01, 0.002, 1),
        (0.01, 0.002, 3),
        (0.01, 0.002, 8),
        (0.05, 0.001, 5),
        (0.13, 0.0007, 11),
    ]:
        g = lambda y: log_size(c, y)                      # noqa: E731
        aff = lambda y: -2.0 + 0.9 * y                    # noqa: E731
        b_log = lambda k: bin_average(a0, delta, w, g, k)  # noqa: E731
        b_aff = lambda k: bin_average(a0, delta, w, aff, k)  # noqa: E731
        worst = max(second_difference(b_log, k) for k in range(0, 20))
        worst_aff = max(abs(second_difference(b_aff, k)) for k in range(0, 20))
        print(f"{a0:10.3f}{delta:12.4f}{w:13d}{worst:26.3e}{worst_aff:12.1e}")
    print("   (log-size column strictly negative everywhere; affine column ~0)")

    # unimodality: once the binned profile descends it never rises again.
    # The chord-referenced deviation is concave (concave minus affine), and it

    a0, b0 = 0.01, 1.0

demos.name: Randomised Falsification Stress Test of the Four Structural Theorems
demos.description: Rather than illustrating the theorems on hand-picked parameters, this demo attempts to break them. Over 1900 pseudo-random parameter draws it checks four claims: (T1) that the fitted quadratic curvature of the log-size profile against the grid-orthogonal quadratic is strictly negative for random bin counts, bin widths and grid centres, while an affine control is zero to floating-point precision relative to the concave signal; (T2) that binned second differences are strictly negative for random offsets, spacings and bin widths, and vanish for an affine control; (T3) that the binned chord gap never ascends after its peak; and (T4) that the vertex satisfies the two-sided logarithmic-mean pin and lies strictly left of the window midpoint, with normalised position strictly below 1/2, over random windows spanning six decades and aspect ratios spanning twelve. The expected and observed outcome is zero violations, and the report prints the largest normalised vertex encountered for comparison with the measured 0.5901.

"""Randomised falsification stress test of the four structural theorems.

Rather than illustrating the theorems on hand-picked parameters, this demo
tries hard to break them.  Over many pseudo-random parameter draws it checks:

  (T1) fitted curvature sign:  for random bin counts n >= 3, random bin widths
       h > 0 and random grid centres m with the grid inside the window, the
       least-squares quadratic coefficient of the log-size profile against the
       grid-orthogonal quadratic is strictly negative -- and exactly zero for
       an affine control;

  (T2) binning invariance:  for random offsets, spacings and bin widths, the
       binned second differences of the log-size profile are strictly negative
       and those of an affine control vanish;

  (T3) unimodality:  the binned chord gap never ascends after its peak;

  (T4) the vertex obstruction and the two-sided pin:  for random windows
       0 < a < b and random aspect ratios c >= 0,
           LM(a,b) <= xi <= LM(a+2c,b+2c) - 2c < (a+b)/2,
       and the normalised vertex is strictly below 1/2 -- never 0.5901.

Any violation is reported; the expected output is zero violations.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

random.seed(20260826)


# --- profile and means -------------------------------------------------------

def log_size(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size_deriv(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return 1.0 / x + 1.0 / (x + 2.0 * c)


def log_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    return (q - p) / (math.log(q) - math.log(p))


def upper_pin(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    p, d = a + 2.0 * c, b - a
    u = d / p
    bracket = (0.5 - u / 12.0 + u * u / 24.0) if u < 1e-4 \
        else 1.0 / math.log1p(u) - 1.0 / u
    return a + d * bracket


def vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    sigma = (log_size(c, b) - log_size(c, a)) / (b - a)
    lo, hi = a, b
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if log_size_deriv(c, mid) > sigma:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


# --- statistics --------------------------------------------------------------

def fitted_curvature(g: Callable[[float], float], n: int, m: float,
                     h: float) -> float:
    off = [i - (n - 1) / 2.0 for i in range(n)]
    v = sum(o * o for o in off) / n
    t = [m + h * o for o in off]
    q = [(x - m) ** 2 - h * h * v for x in t]
    return sum(g(x) * qi for x, qi in zip(t, q)) / sum(qi * qi for qi in q)


def bin_average(g: Callable[[float], float], a: float, delta: float,
                w: int, k: int) -> float:
    return sum(g(a + delta * (k * w + i)) for i in range(w)) / w


# --- trials ------------------------------------------------------------------

def trial_curvature() -> Tuple[bool, str]:
    n = random.randint(3, 90)
    c = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-4, 4)
    h = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-4, -1)
    off_max = (n - 1) / 2.0
    m = h * off_max + 10.0 ** random.uniform(-4, 0)   # keeps the grid positive
    cfit = fitted_curvature(lambda x: log_size(c, x), n, m, h)
    caff = fitted_curvature(lambda x: 2.3 - 0.7 * x, n, m, h)
    # the affine control is exactly zero in exact arithmetic; in floating
    # point compare it against the scale of the concave signal
    ok = cfit < 0.0 and abs(caff) < 1e-6 * max(1.0, abs(cfit))
    return ok, f"n={n} c={c:.2e} h={h:.2e} m={m:.3e} cfit={cfit:.3e} caff={caff:.1e}"


def trial_binning() -> Tuple[bool, str]:
    c = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-4, 4)
    a = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-3, -1)
    delta = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-5, -2)
    w = random.randint(1, 12)
    worst = max(
        bin_average(lambda x: log_size(c, x), a, delta, w, k)
        + bin_average(lambda x: log_size(c, x), a, delta, w, k + 2)
        - 2.0 * bin_average(lambda x: log_size(c, x), a, delta, w, k + 1)
        for k in range(12)
    )
    worst_aff = max(
        abs(bin_average(lambda x: 1.1 + 0.4 * x, a, delta, w, k)
            + bin_average(lambda x: 1.1 + 0.4 * x, a, delta, w, k + 2)
            - 2.0 * bin_average(lambda x: 1.1 + 0.4 * x, a, delta, w, k + 1))
        for k in range(12)
    )
    ok = worst < 0.0 and worst_aff < 1e-10
    return ok, f"c={c:.2e} a={a:.2e} delta={delta:.2e} w={w} worst={worst:.2e}"


def trial_unimodal() -> Tuple[bool, str]:
    c = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-3, 3)
    a = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-3, -1)
    b = 1.0
    sigma = (log_size(c, b) - log_size(c, a)) / (b - a)
    gap = lambda x: log_size(c, x) - (log_size(c, a) + (x - a) * sigma)  # noqa: E731
    w = random.randint(1, 6)
    nb = 40
    delta = (b - a) / (w * nb + 1)
    seq: List[float] = [bin_average(gap, a, delta, w, k) for k in range(nb)]
    peak = max(range(nb), key=lambda k: seq[k])
    ascents = sum(1 for k in range(peak, nb - 1) if seq[k + 1] > seq[k] + 1e-15)
    return ascents == 0, f"c={c:.2e} a={a:.2e} w={w} peak={peak} ascents={ascents}"


def trial_vertex() -> Tuple[bool, str]:
    a = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-6, 0)
    b = a * 10.0 ** random.uniform(0.05, 6)
    c = 10.0 ** random.uniform(-6, 6) if random.random() < 0.9 else 0.0
    xi = vertex(max(c, 1e-300), a, b)
    lo = log_mean(a, b)
    hi = upper_pin(c, a, b) if c > 0 else lo
    mid = (a + b) / 2.0
    nrm = (xi - a) / (b - a)
    tol = 1e-9 * max(1.0, abs(mid))
    ok = (lo <= xi + tol) and (xi <= hi + tol) and (xi < mid) and (nrm < 0.5)
    return ok, (f"a={a:.2e} b={b:.2e} c={c:.2e} LM={lo:.6g} xi={xi:.6g} "
                f"pin={hi:.6g} mid={mid:.6g} norm={nrm:.4f}")


def run(name: str, trial: Callable[[], Tuple[bool, str]], n: int) -> int:
    fails = 0
    worst_msg = ""
    for _ in range(n):
        ok, msg = trial()
        if not ok:
            fails += 1
            worst_msg = msg
    status = "PASS" if fails == 0 else f"FAIL ({fails}/{n})"
    print(f"  {name:<46}{status}")
    if worst_msg:
        print(f"      counterexample candidate: {worst_msg}")
    return fails


def main() -> None:
    print("Randomised falsification stress test")
    print("-" * 62)
    total = 0
    total += run("T1  fitted curvature sign / affine control", trial_curvature, 400)
    total += run("T2  bin-average second differences", trial_binning, 400)
    total += run("T3  unimodality of the binned gap", trial_unimodal, 300)
    total += run("T4  vertex pin and left-of-centre bound", trial_vertex, 800)
    print("-" * 62)
    print(f"  total violations: {total}")
    print("  maximum normalised vertex seen over all draws: "
          f"{max((vertex(1e-3, a, 1.0) - a) / (1.0 - a) for a in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.99]):.6f}")
    print("  (the theoretical ceiling is 1/2; the measured apex is 0.5901)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Monotone Bisection for the Chord-Gap Vertex
algorithms.description: Locates the unique point ξ in (a,b) at which the log-size profile's slope equals the chord slope, i.e. 1/ξ + 1/(ξ+2c) = (L_c(b)-L_c(a))/(b-a). Correctness does not rely on any smoothness assumption beyond what is proved: the slope function x ↦ 1/x + 1/(x+2c) is strictly decreasing on (0,∞), so the residual has exactly one sign change on the window, and the mean value theorem guarantees it is bracketed by the endpoints. Bisection is therefore unconditionally convergent with bracket width (b-a)·2^{-k} after k steps; reaching double precision takes about 50 iterations, each costing O(1) arithmetic operations, so the total cost is O(log(1/tol)). The same monotonicity that makes the algorithm correct is the one that makes the vertex unique, so the routine is a faithful numerical witness of the uniqueness theorem.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  aspect ratio c ≥ 0, window 0 < a < b, tolerance tol
OUTPUT the unique ξ ∈ (a,b) with L_c'(ξ) = chord slope

1.  σ ← (L_c(b) − L_c(a)) / (b − a)          // chord slope
2.  lo ← a ;  hi ← b
3.  while hi − lo > tol do
4.       mid ← (lo + hi) / 2
5.       if 1/mid + 1/(mid + 2c) > σ then      // slope still too steep
6.            lo ← mid                          //   move right
7.       else
8.            hi ← mid                          //   move left
9.  return (lo + hi) / 2

INVARIANT  L_c'(lo) ≥ σ ≥ L_c'(hi), maintained because L_c' is strictly
           decreasing; hence the bracket always contains the unique root.

algorithms.name: Closed-Form Grid-Orthogonal Quadratic Fit of the Curvature Statistic
algorithms.description: Computes the least-squares quadratic coefficient of a profile sampled on an equal-width bin grid, without any explicit orthogonalisation. With n bins of width h centred at m, put o_i = i − (n−1)/2, t_i = m + h·o_i and V(n) = (1/n)∑o_i²; the quadratic q(y) = (y − m)² − h²V(n) then satisfies ∑q(t_i) = 0 and ∑t_i q(t_i) = 0 for every h and every m — the first by definition of V, the second because the odd moments of a symmetric grid vanish under the reflection i ↦ n−1−i. The statistic is ∑g(t_i)q(t_i) / ∑q(t_i)², computed in a single O(n) pass with O(1) memory. Because the numerator is provably non-positive for concave profiles, strictly negative for strictly concave ones, and exactly zero for affine ones, the routine doubles as a falsification test: a positive output on data believed concave indicates a modelling error rather than a fitting artefact. The module also reports the two orthogonality residuals as a numerical self-check.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  profile g, bin count n ≥ 3, grid centre m, bin width h > 0
OUTPUT the least-squares quadratic coefficient of g on the grid

1.  for i = 0 .. n−1:  o_i ← i − (n−1)/2
2.  V ← (1/n) · ∑ o_i²                       // mean square centred offset
3.  for i = 0 .. n−1:  t_i ← m + h·o_i        // bin centres
4.  for i = 0 .. n−1:  q_i ← (t_i − m)² − h²V // = (t_i−r₁)(t_i−r₂),
                                              //   r₁,₂ = m ∓ h√V
5.  assert |∑ q_i| ≈ 0  and  |∑ t_i q_i| ≈ 0  // orthogonality, free of charge
6.  num ← ∑ g(t_i)·q_i
7.  den ← ∑ q_i²                             // > 0 whenever n ≥ 3
8.  return num / den

COST  O(n) time, O(1) extra memory.
GUARANTEE  g concave ⇒ output ≤ 0 ; g strictly concave ⇒ output < 0 ;
           g affine ⇒ output = 0 exactly.
algorithms.code:
"""Least-squares quadratic curvature on an arbitrary equal-width bin grid.

The grid-orthogonal quadratic is available in closed form, so no explicit
Gram-Schmidt is needed:  with n bins of width h centred at m,

    o_i = i - (n-1)/2,   t_i = m + h o_i,   V(n) = (1/n) sum o_i^2,
    q(y) = (y - m)^2 - h^2 V(n) = (y - r1)(y - r2),  r1,2 = m -/+ h sqrt(V(n)),

one has  sum q(t_i) = 0  and  sum t_i q(t_i) = 0  for every h and every m.
For a concave profile the numerator sum g(t_i) q(t_i) is then non-positive,
strictly negative if the profile is strictly concave; for an affine profile it
is exactly zero.  The routine is therefore both an estimator and a
falsification test.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


def centred_offsets(n: int) -> List[float]:
    return [i - (n - 1) / 2.0 for i in range(n)]


def grid_variance(n: int) -> float:
    off = centred_offsets(n)
    return sum(o * o for o in off) / n


def bin_centres(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> List[float]:
    return [m + h * o for o in centred_offsets(n)]


def orthogonal_roots(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    rho = h * math.sqrt(grid_variance(n))
    return m - rho, m + rho


def fitted_curvature(
    g: Callable[[float], float], n: int, m: float, h: float
) -> float:
    """Least-squares quadratic coefficient of g on the (n, m, h) bin grid."""
    if n < 3:
        raise ValueError("need at least three bins for a witness point")
    t = bin_centres(n, m, h)
    v = grid_variance(n)
    q = [(x - m) ** 2 - h * h * v for x in t]
    num = sum(g(x) * qi for x, qi in zip(t, q))
    den = sum(qi * qi for qi in q)
    return num / den


def orthogonality_residuals(n: int, m: float, h: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Numerical check of the two orthogonality relations (both ~0)."""
    t = bin_centres(n, m, h)
    v = grid_variance(n)
    q = [(x - m) ** 2 - h * h * v for x in t]
    return sum(q), sum(x * qi for x, qi in zip(t, q))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    c = 1.0
    log_size = lambda x: math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2 * c)   # noqa: E731
    affine = lambda x: 3.0 + 1.7 * x                          # noqa: E731
    print(f"{'n':>5}{'h':>9}{'m':>8}{'c_fit(log-size)':>19}"
          f"{'c_fit(affine)':>16}{'orth resid':>14}")
    for n, m, h in [(8, .5, .05), (16, .5, .05), (32, .4, .02),
                    (64, .35, .01), (64, .6, .012), (17, .55, .03)]:
        r0, r1 = orthogonality_residuals(n, m, h)
        print(f"{n:5d}{h:9.3f}{m:8.2f}"
              f"{fitted_curvature(log_size, n, m, h):19.8f}"
              f"{fitted_curvature(affine, n, m, h):16.2e}"
              f"{max(abs(r0), abs(r1)):14.1e}")

algorithms.name: Bin-Width Permutation and Grid-Shift Probe by Discrete Second Differences
algorithms.description: Implements the discretisation robustness probe directly. For a sample grid s_i = a + δi and bin width w it forms the bin averages b_k = (1/w)∑_{i<w} g(s_{kw+i}) and their discrete second differences b_k + b_{k+2} − 2b_{k+1}, then sweeps a family of (offset, spacing, bin width) settings and reports the worst (largest) value in each. The underlying theorem is that sample (k+1)w+i is exactly the midpoint of samples kw+i and (k+2)w+i, so midpoint concavity applied w times and averaged gives a non-positive second difference at every setting, strictly negative for strictly concave profiles and exactly zero for affine ones. A second routine audits unimodality by locating the peak of the binned sequence and counting ascents strictly after it: discrete concavity forces that count to be zero, so no bin-width permutation can split a peak in two. Cost is O(w) evaluations per bin, hence O(n·w) for an n-bin sweep.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT  profile g, list of settings (a, δ, w, n_bins)
OUTPUT worst second difference per setting; unimodality audit

PROCEDURE BinAverage(g, a, δ, w, k):
1.   return (1/w) · ∑_{i=0}^{w−1} g(a + δ·(k·w + i))

PROCEDURE SecondDifferences(g, a, δ, w, n_bins):
2.   for k = 0 .. n_bins−1:  b_k ← BinAverage(g, a, δ, w, k)
3.   return [ b_k + b_{k+2} − 2·b_{k+1}  :  k = 0 .. n_bins−3 ]

PROCEDURE UnimodalityAudit(g, a, δ, w, n_bins):
4.   compute b_0 .. b_{n_bins−1} as above
5.   peak ← argmax_k b_k
6.   ascents ← #{ k ≥ peak : b_{k+1} > b_k }
7.   return (peak, ascents)      // theorem: ascents = 0 for concave g

FOR each setting (a, δ, w, n_bins):
8.   report max SecondDifferences(g, a, δ, w, n_bins)
     // concave profile  ⇒ strictly negative
     // affine  control  ⇒ zero to machine precision
algorithms.code:
"""Bin-width permutation and grid-shift probe via discrete second differences.

For a sample grid s_i = a + delta * i and bin width w, the bin averages

    b_k = (1/w) sum_{i<w} g(a + delta (k w + i))

satisfy b_k + b_{k+2} - 2 b_{k+1} <= 0 for every concave g, at every offset a,
every spacing delta and every bin width w -- strictly for strictly concave g.
An affine profile gives exactly 0.  Discrete concavity forces unimodality: once
the binned sequence turns down it never turns back up, so a single peak.

This module sweeps a family of (a, delta, w) settings and reports the worst
(largest) second difference in each, plus a unimodality audit.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple


def bin_average(
    g: Callable[[float], float], a: float, delta: float, w: int, k: int
) -> float:
    return sum(g(a + delta * (k * w + i)) for i in range(w)) / w


def second_differences(
    g: Callable[[float], float], a: float, delta: float, w: int, n_bins: int
) -> List[float]:
    b = [bin_average(g, a, delta, w, k) for k in range(n_bins)]
    return [b[k] + b[k + 2] - 2.0 * b[k + 1] for k in range(n_bins - 2)]


def unimodality_audit(
    g: Callable[[float], float], a: float, delta: float, w: int, n_bins: int
) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (peak index, number of ascents strictly after the peak)."""
    b = [bin_average(g, a, delta, w, k) for k in range(n_bins)]
    peak = max(range(n_bins), key=lambda k: b[k])
    ascents = sum(1 for k in range(peak, n_bins - 1) if b[k + 1] > b[k])
    return peak, ascents


def probe(
    g: Callable[[float], float], settings: List[Tuple[float, float, int, int]]
) -> Dict[Tuple[float, float, int], float]:
    """Worst second difference over a family of (a, delta, w, n_bins)."""
    out: Dict[Tuple[float, float, int], float] = {}
    for a, delta, w, n_bins in settings:
        out[(a, delta, w)] = max(second_differences(g, a, delta, w, n_bins))
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    c, a0, b0 = 1.0, 0.01, 1.0
    log_size = lambda x: math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2 * c)   # noqa: E731
    slope = (log_size(b0) - log_size(a0)) / (b0 - a0)
    gap = lambda x: log_size(x) - (log_size(a0) + (x - a0) * slope)  # noqa: E731
    affine = lambda x: -2.0 + 0.9 * x                         # noqa: E731

    settings = [(0.01, 0.002, 1, 22), (0.01, 0.002, 3, 22),
                (0.01, 0.002, 8, 22), (0.05, 0.001, 5, 22),
                (0.13, 0.0007, 11, 22)]
    print("worst second difference (log-size / affine control):")
    for key, val in probe(log_size, settings).items():
        aff = probe(affine, [(key[0], key[1], key[2], 22)])[key]
        print(f"   a={key[0]:<6} delta={key[1]:<8} w={key[2]:<3} "
              f"-> {val:12.3e}   affine {aff:9.1e}")
    peak, ascents = unimodality_audit(gap, a0, 0.004, 4, 60)
    print(f"unimodality audit on the chord gap: peak bin {peak}, "
          f"ascents after peak {ascents}")

visualizations.name: The Geometric Hump and the Vertex Obstruction
visualizations.description: Two panels. On the left, the log-size profile log x + log(x + 2c) is drawn for four aspect ratios together with the endpoint chord, showing directly how concavity lifts the curve above the straight-line reference. On the right, the resulting chord gap is normalised to unit height for each aspect ratio and overlaid with vertical markers: each curve's own vertex, the window midpoint, and the measured apex at relative position 0.5901. The figure makes the obstruction visible at a glance — every vertex falls to the left of the midpoint line while the measured apex falls to the right of it, and no choice of aspect ratio moves a vertex across.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the chord-referenced hump and the vertex obstruction.

Left panel: the log-size profile L_c(x) = log x + log(x + 2c) with its endpoint
chord, for several aspect ratios.  Right panel: the resulting chord gap, with
its vertex, the window midpoint, and the measured relative apex 0.5901 marked.
The point of the figure is that every vertex sits strictly left of the midpoint
while the measurement sits strictly right of it.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def log_size(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size_deriv(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return 1.0 / x + 1.0 / (x + 2.0 * c)


def vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    sigma = (log_size(c, b) - log_size(c, a)) / (b - a)
    lo, hi = a, b
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if log_size_deriv(c, mid) > sigma:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def main() -> None:
    a, b = 0.01, 1.0
    xs: List[float] = [a + (b - a) * i / 800.0 for i in range(801)]
    aspects = [0.0, 0.05, 0.5, 5.0]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    for c in aspects:
        cc = max(c, 1e-12)
        ys = [log_size(cc, x) for x in xs]
        ax1.plot(xs, ys, lw=1.8, label=f"$c={c}$")
    ch = [log_size(1e-12, a) + (x - a) / (b - a)
          * (log_size(1e-12, b) - log_size(1e-12, a)) for x in xs]
    ax1.plot(xs, ch, "k--", lw=1.2, label="endpoint chord ($c=0$)")
    ax1.set_title(r"log-size profile $L_c(x)=\log x+\log(x+2c)$")
    ax1.set_xlabel("relative window position $x$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("log-size (up to an additive constant)")
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

    for c in aspects:
        cc = max(c, 1e-12)
        sigma = (log_size(cc, b) - log_size(cc, a)) / (b - a)
        gap = [log_size(cc, x) - (log_size(cc, a) + (x - a) * sigma)
               for x in xs]
        gmax = max(gap)
        line, = ax2.plot(xs, [g / gmax for g in gap], lw=1.8, label=f"$c={c}$")
        xi = vertex(cc, a, b)
        ax2.axvline(xi, color=line.get_color(), ls=":", lw=1.0)

    ax2.axvline((a + b) / 2, color="k", ls="--", lw=1.4,
                label="window midpoint")
    ax2.axvline(a + 0.5901 * (b - a), color="crimson", lw=2.2,
                label="measured apex $0.5901$")
    ax2.set_title("chord gap (normalised): every vertex is left of centre")
    ax2.set_xlabel("relative window position $x$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("gap / peak gap")
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    fig.suptitle("The geometric hump of $j^2-N$ and the vertex obstruction",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("hump_and_vertex.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote hump_and_vertex.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Rigidity of the Vertex and the Collapse Toward the Left Edge
visualizations.description: Two panels. The left panel plots the vertex as a function of the aspect ratio over thirteen decades, shaded between its two pins: the aspect-ratio-free lower pin given by the logarithmic mean of the window endpoints and the shifted upper pin, with the window midpoint marked. The vertex hugs the lower pin at both extremes and bulges only mildly in the middle, which is the visual content of the rigidity theorem. The right panel plots the normalised vertex in the sieve regime a = 1/M, b = 1 as the window length M grows over nine decades, against the bound 1/log M, the window centre at 1/2 and the measured apex 0.5901; the geometric vertex descends steadily toward the left edge while the measurement sits above the centre line, so the discrepancy widens with problem size rather than closing.

"""Visualisation: the two-sided logarithmic-mean pin on the vertex.

Left panel: the vertex as a function of the aspect ratio c, plotted with the
aspect-ratio-free lower pin LM(a,b), the shifted upper pin
LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c, and the window midpoint.  The vertex is trapped in a band
whose lower edge does not move at all with c -- which is why it is numerically
so insensitive to c.

Right panel: the normalised vertex in the sieve regime a = 1/M, b = 1 as the
window length M grows, together with the bound 1/log M and the measured apex
0.5901.  The geometric vertex runs toward the left edge; the measurement sits
above the midpoint.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def log_size(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return math.log(x) + math.log(x + 2.0 * c)


def log_size_deriv(c: float, x: float) -> float:
    return 1.0 / x + 1.0 / (x + 2.0 * c)


def log_mean(p: float, q: float) -> float:
    return (q - p) / (math.log(q) - math.log(p))


def upper_pin(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """LM(a+2c, b+2c) - 2c, evaluated stably for large c."""
    p, d = a + 2.0 * c, b - a
    u = d / p
    bracket = (0.5 - u / 12.0 + u * u / 24.0) if u < 1e-4 \
        else 1.0 / math.log1p(u) - 1.0 / u
    return a + d * bracket


def vertex(c: float, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    sigma = (log_size(c, b) - log_size(c, a)) / (b - a)
    lo, hi = a, b
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if log_size_deriv(c, mid) > sigma:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def main() -> None:
    a, b = 0.01, 1.0
    cs: List[float] = [10.0 ** (-4 + 13 * i / 300.0) for i in range(301)]
    xis = [vertex(c, a, b) for c in cs]
    lows = [log_mean(a, b) for _ in cs]
    ups = [min(upper_pin(c, a, b), 0.505) for c in cs]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    ax1.fill_between(cs, lows, ups, color="steelblue", alpha=0.15,
                     label="admissible band (two-sided pin)")
    ax1.plot(cs, xis, lw=2.2, color="navy", label=r"vertex $\xi$")
    ax1.plot(cs, lows, "g--", lw=1.6, label=r"lower pin $\mathrm{LM}(a,b)$")
    ax1.plot(cs, ups, "r--", lw=1.2,
             label=r"upper pin $\mathrm{LM}(a+2c,b+2c)-2c$")
    ax1.axhline((a + b) / 2, color="k", ls=":", lw=1.4, label="midpoint")
    ax1.set_xscale("log")
    ax1.set_xlabel("aspect ratio $c=\\sqrt{N}/M$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("vertex position on $[a,b]=[0.01,1]$")
    ax1.set_title("the vertex is pinned between two logarithmic means")
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

    Ms = [10.0 ** (1 + 9 * i / 200.0) for i in range(201)]
    norm = [(log_mean(1.0 / M, 1.0) - 1.0 / M) / (1.0 - 1.0 / M) for M in Ms]
    bound = [1.0 / math.log(M) for M in Ms]
    ax2.plot(Ms, norm, lw=2.2, color="navy", label="normalised vertex")
    ax2.plot(Ms, bound, "g--", lw=1.4, label=r"bound $1/\log M$")
    ax2.axhline(0.5, color="k", ls=":", lw=1.4, label="window centre")
    ax2.axhline(0.5901, color="crimson", lw=2.0, label="measured apex 0.5901")
    ax2.set_xscale("log")
    ax2.set_ylim(0, 0.7)
    ax2.set_xlabel("window length $M$ (sieve regime $a=1/M$, $b=1$)")
    ax2.set_ylabel("relative vertex position")
    ax2.set_title("the geometric vertex collapses onto the left edge")
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    fig.suptitle("Rigidity of the vertex, and why $0.5901$ is out of reach",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("vertex_pin.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote vertex_pin.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.description: An interactive test bench for the discretisation robustness probe. The user selects one of four profiles — the log-size profile, its chord gap, an affine control, or a convex foil — and then permutes the bin count, the bin width, the grid centre and the aspect ratio. The canvas draws the binned profile as bars with the peak bin highlighted, overlaid with the grid-orthogonal quadratic q(y) = (y − m)² − h²V(n) that defines the curvature statistic. Live readouts show the fitted curvature, the worst discrete second difference, the peak bin index, the number of ascents after the peak, and the orthogonality residual of the quadratic. The lesson emerges from experiment: for the concave settings the curvature and every second difference stay strictly negative and the ascent count stays at zero no matter how the grid is permuted; the affine control returns machine zero at every setting, so the binning cannot manufacture curvature; and the convex foil flips both diagnostics honestly, confirming that the statistics report the curvature that is actually present.
